title: Memoized search reuses previously computed states
summary: On the first visit, memoized search computes and caches each non-base state along the left branch. When a right branch reaches the same state, its cached value still contributes to the parent’s sum.
context: Again counting ways to climb stairs by taking 1 or 2 steps at a time, with base cases dp[1] = 1 and dp[2] = 2, memoized search introduces an array mem to record computed non-base state values: base cases return immediately, while non-base states check mem first and expand further only if not yet recorded.
description: In the figure, the main first-time computation chain runs dp[9] → dp[8] → dp[7] → ... → dp[3], with dp[6] through dp[4] condensed as ellipses; dp[3] then splits into the base cases dp[2] and dp[1]. On the right, scissors icons explicitly mark cached reuse at dp[7], dp[6], and dp[5], while remaining reuse points are summarized by ellipses. Filling in the omitted segment from the code also reuses dp[4] inside dp[6] and dp[3] inside dp[5]; the right subproblem dp[2] of dp[4] returns directly as a base case rather than a cache hit.

For example, computing dp[9] first completes its left subproblem dp[8], during which dp[7] is already computed and stored; when evaluating the right subproblem (dp[7] marked with scissors), the search reads the cached value directly without expanding it again, and that value still contributes to the sum for dp[9].
The two tables below list the three reuse relationships explicitly shown in the figure and how the code handles base cases, first-time computations, and cache hits.

frames.title: Memoized search reuses previously computed states
frames.explanation: Each non-base state is expanded and computed only once, and repeated lookups return the cached value directly, reducing the time complexity to O(n).
